text:
This section examines Experiment G — Exact
v4 neural ground

truth from first principles. Keep two
questions separate: does changing

the order change the measured outcome, and
does the proposed

search method beat a matched alternative
at the same distinct-evaluation

budget? Design changes: residual
bottleneck blocks; initialization seeded

permutation and trial; all 120 orderings
enumerated; three deterministic

trials per ordering; 50–100 Adam steps;
learning rate 0.1. XOR-v4:

optimum 1.0000, eight of 120 orderings
optimal, landscape standard deviation

0.120, prism 100% hit rate. Parity-v4:
optimum 0.9583, two of

120 optimal, standard deviation 0.098,
prism 40% hit rate, mean

regret 0.0333. Determinism: repeat
evaluations matched; later 103 accidental

duplicate evaluations across restarts also
matched. Visual: fill the

120-cell permutation grid, mark optima,
then run the search pointer

over the cached table. Now read evidence
panel G-landscape. The

axes, units, and sample are stated on
screen. The sample

represented here is all 120 orderings. Raw
observations remain visible

wherever the artifact provides them.
Censored observations stay marked at

the cap rather than becoming invented
hitting times, and sampled

landscapes leave unobserved permutations
blank. The supported finding is:

XOR-v4: optimum 1.0000, eight of 120
orderings optimal, landscape standard

deviation 0.120, prism 100% hit rate. The
broader claim not

established here is: The conclusion is
scoped to the recorded

evaluator, landscape, and budget. This
evidence changed the program as

follows: Carry this constraint into the
next experiment and compare

methods at equal cost. The distinction is
part of the

result. A large ordering effect does not
automatically imply an

evolutionary-search advantage, and
almost-sure convergence does not promise
practical efficiency.
